overview.text: A neuron, or nerve cell, is a specialized cell that receives and sends information, making it a basic signaling unit of the nervous system. Its cell body contains the nucleus; branching dendrites receive signals, while an axon carries electrical impulses away from the cell body. Neurons vary in shape and role: sensory neurons convey information about stimuli, while motor neurons carry messages to muscles. Within a neuron, signals travel electrically along the axon. At many synapses, the axon terminal releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, which cross a small gap and affect a neighboring cell. This combination of electrical signaling within neurons and chemical signaling between cells helps connect neurons into circuits for sensation, movement, and communication between the brain and body.

key_facts.text: A typical neuron has a cell body with a nucleus, signal-receiving dendrites, and a message-carrying axon; neurons’ shapes can vary with their roles and locations.
Sensory neurons send information about stimuli toward the brain; motor neurons carry messages that help generate movement by activating muscles.
A neuron carries an electrical signal along its axon; at many synapses, chemical neurotransmitters carry the message across a small gap to another cell.
In most circuits, a synapse includes an axon ending, part of a neighboring neuron such as a dendrite, and the narrow gap between them.
Glia are nervous-system cells distinct from neurons; among their roles, they provide support and produce myelin insulation that helps nerve impulses travel.
